questions.question: A bakery splits cake production into mixing, baking, icing and boxing, each done by a different worker. Output rises at first, but later absenteeism and turnover climb. What does this illustrate?

options.A: Departmentalization by process, which always raises morale over time
options.B: Specialization's efficiency, and its human costs if overdone
options.C: A wider span of control, which overloads each of the supervisors
options.D: Decentralization, which leaves workers unsure who makes the decisions

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Work specialization subdivides tasks into separate jobs; it boosts efficiency through repetition and easier training, but carried too far it brings boredom, fatigue, stress, poor quality, absenteeism and turnover. (Ch 13: Work Specialization)
**Why not A:** Grouping by process doesn't guarantee morale; the issue is overly narrow, repetitive jobs.
**Why not C:** Nothing here concerns how many people report to each supervisor.
**Why not D:** The change was in how tasks were subdivided, not where decisions are made.

questions.question: A consumer-goods company puts one executive in charge of everything related to each of its brands worldwide. Which departmentalization is this, and what's its main advantage?

options.A: Process; homogeneous grouping by each phase of production
options.B: Functional; efficiency from grouping people with common skills
options.C: Product; clear accountability for each product's results
options.D: Customer; specialists who meet each market's shared needs

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Product departmentalization groups activities by product under a single manager (as at Procter & Gamble), increasing accountability for product performance. (Ch 13: Departmentalization)
**Why not A:** Process departmentalization groups by production phase, not by brand.
**Why not B:** That's the advantage of functional grouping, which organizes by function, not product.
**Why not D:** Customer departmentalization groups by type of customer, not by brand.

questions.question: To get a driver's licence, you're validated by one division, processed by the licensing department, then pay at the treasury department. Which form of departmentalization is this?

options.A: Functional departmentalization
options.B: Geographical departmentalization
options.C: Customer departmentalization
options.D: Process departmentalization

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Process departmentalization groups activities by each phase of processing, and it can be used to process customers as well as products. (Ch 13: Process Departmentalization)
**Why not A:** Functional departmentalization groups people by the functions they perform, not by sequential steps a customer moves through.
**Why not B:** Geographical departmentalization groups activities by territory or region.
**Why not C:** Customer departmentalization groups activities by type of customer served.

questions.question: An engineer reports to both a project manager and a functional head, who keep giving her conflicting priorities. Which structural principle has been broken?

options.A: Work specialization
options.B: Unity of command
options.C: Formalization
options.D: Span of control

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Unity of command says a person should have one and only one superior to whom they're directly responsible; when it's broken, employees may face conflicting demands from several superiors. (Ch 13: Chain of Command)
**Why not A:** Work specialization is the degree to which tasks are subdivided into separate jobs.
**Why not C:** Formalization is the degree to which jobs are standardized.
**Why not D:** Span of control is the number of employees reporting to one manager.

questions.question: Two firms each have about 4100 front-line employees. One uses spans of control of 4; the other uses spans of 8. What's the main trade-off between them?

options.A: Wider spans cut costs, but can weaken support if they get too wide
options.B: Narrow spans cut costs and speed up vertical communication
options.C: Span size has no effect on costs or on the number of levels
options.D: Wider spans need more levels and many more managers overall

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** The span of 8 needs two fewer levels and about 800 fewer managers, saving millions; but once supervisors lack time to lead and support, wider spans reduce effectiveness. Narrow spans are costly, slow communication and encourage overly tight supervision. (Ch 13: Span of Control, Exhibit 13-2)
**Why not B:** Narrow spans add costly levels and make vertical communication slower.
**Why not C:** The wider span saves two levels and roughly 800 managers.
**Why not D:** Wider spans need fewer levels and fewer managers.

questions.question: A 2013 study compared centralized and decentralized organizations. Which kind of error is each better at avoiding?

options.A: Both are equally good at avoiding every kind of error
options.B: Decentralized firms avoid both kinds of errors equally well
options.C: Centralized avoids lost chances; decentralized, bad choices
options.D: Centralized avoids bad choices; decentralized, lost chances

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Centralized organizations are better at avoiding commission errors (bad choices), while decentralized organizations are better at avoiding omission errors (lost opportunities). (Ch 13: Centralization and Decentralization)
**Why not A:** The study found each structure better at avoiding a different type of error.
**Why not B:** Centralized firms were better at avoiding bad choices.
**Why not C:** This reverses the findings.

questions.question: A fast-food chain scripts exactly how staff greet customers, count change and thank them, and managers check a list of these behaviours. Which structural element is high here?

options.A: Decentralization
options.B: Departmentalization
options.C: Span of control
options.D: Formalization

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Formalization is the degree to which jobs are standardized: explicit job descriptions, many rules and clearly defined procedures, so the same input is handled the same way every time. (Ch 13: Formalization)
**Why not A:** Decentralization pushes decision making down; here behaviour is scripted from above.
**Why not B:** Departmentalization concerns how jobs are grouped, not how scripted they are.
**Why not C:** Span of control concerns how many people report to a manager.

questions.question: A big retailer gives store managers much more say over what merchandise to stock so they can compete with local shops. What trend does this reflect, and why?

options.A: Decentralization, as local managers know more about problems
options.B: Formalization, since standard rules now govern every purchase
options.C: Work specialization, since buyers now focus on one product line
options.D: Centralization, since top managers can coordinate all buying

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** To make organizations more flexible and responsive, decision making has been decentralized to lower-level managers, who are closer to the action and typically know more about problems than top managers. (Ch 13: Centralization and Decentralization)
**Why not B:** Stocking decisions became more discretionary, not more rule-bound.
**Why not C:** The change concerns who makes decisions, not how tasks are subdivided.
**Why not D:** Giving store managers more discretion is decentralization.

questions.question: A start-up has two levels, wide spans, little formalization, and its founder makes every decision. As it grows past 200 people, decisions slow to a crawl. What does the chapter say about this structure?

options.A: A matrix structure fails when the founder has two bosses
options.B: A virtual organization slows down once it stops outsourcing
options.C: A bureaucracy handles growth well through standard procedures
options.D: A simple structure struggles to cope as a firm grows

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** The simple structure is fast, flexible and cheap with clear accountability, but as a firm grows its low formalization and high centralization overload the top; it's also risky, since everything depends on one person. (Ch 13: The Simple Structure)
**Why not A:** Nothing here involves a dual chain of command.
**Why not B:** The firm isn't a network of outsourced partners.
**Why not C:** The firm described is a simple structure, not a bureaucracy.

questions.question: A family firm's founder wants his eldest son to succeed him, although a daughter may be the stronger candidate. What does the chapter say about succession in family businesses?

options.A: It needs no governance, since family ties settle conflicts
options.B: It works best when the eldest child takes over automatically
options.C: It often fails when emotion, not suitability, picks the next heir
options.D: It succeeds whenever the business is listed on an exchange

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Succession in family businesses often doesn't work because personal and emotional factors, rather than suitability, determine the next leader; good governance (direction, values and accepted policies) helps manage such conflicts. (Ch 13: The Family Business)
**Why not A:** Family businesses need governance for the business, the family and the owners.
**Why not B:** Choosing by birth order rather than suitability is exactly what tends to cause problems.
**Why not D:** Being publicly listed doesn't solve succession problems.

questions.question: A bank processes routine transactions with specialized staff, strict rules and decisions that follow the chain of command. What are the main strength and main weakness of this structure?

options.A: Fast innovation, but high costs from duplicated specialist staff
options.B: Clear dual reporting, but frequent power struggles over staff
options.C: Great flexibility, but unclear roles and constant reorganizing
options.D: Efficient routines, but rigid with cases that break the rules

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** A bureaucracy performs standardized activities very efficiently, with economies of scale and less need for talented middle managers; its weaknesses are silos where unit goals override organizational goals, and obsessive rule-following when cases don't fit. (Ch 13: The Bureaucracy)
**Why not A:** Bureaucracies minimize duplication; their strength is efficient routine work, not innovation.
**Why not B:** Dual reporting and power struggles describe the matrix structure.
**Why not C:** Constant flux and unclear roles describe virtual organizations.

questions.question: In a business faculty, a professor teaching an MBA course reports to both the accounting chair and the director of master's programs. Which structure is this, and what's its main risk?

options.A: A bureaucracy; silos and obsessive concern with rules
options.B: A virtual network; weak cultural alignment among partners
options.C: A simple structure; overload on the single top decision maker
options.D: A matrix; confusion, power struggles and role stress

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** A matrix combines functional and product departmentalization with a dual chain of command; it fosters coordination, but breaking unity of command creates confusion, power struggles and stress from role conflict and ambiguity. (Ch 13: The Matrix Structure, Exhibit 13-3)
**Why not A:** Reporting to two bosses is the defining feature of a matrix, not a bureaucracy.
**Why not B:** The professor works inside one organization with a dual chain of command.
**Why not C:** A simple structure centralizes authority in one person; this has two reporting lines.

questions.question: An aerospace firm with many complex, interdependent projects adopts a matrix structure. What does it mainly gain?

options.A: Less stress, since roles and expectations are clearer
options.B: Fewer power struggles, since rules are fixed in advance
options.C: Better coordination and faster flow of information
options.D: Clear unity of command with a single boss for each employee

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** The matrix's strength is fostering coordination when there are many complex, interdependent activities: information reaches those who need it faster, 'bureaupathologies' shrink and specialists are allocated efficiently. (Ch 13: Advantages of a Matrix Structure)
**Why not A:** The matrix tends to increase stress, role conflict and ambiguity.
**Why not B:** The matrix tends to foster power struggles between managers.
**Why not D:** The matrix breaks unity of command by giving employees two bosses.

questions.question: A food company with only 28 employees outsources manufacturing, procurement, shipping and quality control, keeping a small executive core. What is this design, and what's a key drawback?

options.A: A virtual organization; roles and goals can be unclear
options.B: A matrix; employees must report to two different bosses
options.C: A bureaucracy; standardized rules slow down every single decision
options.D: A simple structure; one owner makes all of the decisions

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** In a virtual organization a small core outsources major functions; it's flexible and saves on offices and hierarchy, but constant flux leaves roles, goals and responsibilities unclear, invites politics, and low interaction can erode shared culture. (Ch 13: The Virtual Organization, Exhibit 13-4)
**Why not B:** Nothing here involves a dual chain of command.
**Why not C:** Outsourcing nearly everything from a small core is a virtual organization.
**Why not D:** The defining feature is outsourcing to a network of other firms.

questions.question: A CEO wants to flatten the hierarchy, create cross-hierarchical teams, use 360-degree appraisals and rotate people across functions. Which design is he pursuing, and what's the catch?

options.A: A bureaucracy; it concentrates power in too few hands
options.B: A boundaryless organization; it's hard to manage
options.C: A matrix; it adds a second chain of command for all staff
options.D: A simple structure; it depends entirely on one person

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** The boundaryless organization seeks to eliminate the chain of command, have limitless spans and replace departments with empowered teams; it's hard to manage because political and authority boundaries resist change and coordination is demanding. (Ch 13: The Boundaryless Organization)
**Why not A:** These moves break down hierarchy, the opposite of bureaucracy.
**Why not C:** The goal is to remove chains of command, not add a second one.
**Why not D:** Cross-hierarchical teams and 360 appraisals spread decisions widely.

questions.question: A company cuts 20% of its staff without restructuring how work gets done. What does research suggest about the results?

options.A: Morale improves, since remaining staff feel more secure
options.B: Profits rise steadily, since wage costs are permanently lower
options.C: Profits and stock prices usually decline afterward
options.D: Turnover falls, since survivors value their jobs more

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Firms that downsize to sharpen strategic focus often see stock gains, but those that only cut employees without restructuring usually see profits and stock prices decline; survivors may be stressed and less committed, and talent may leave. (Ch 13: The Leaner Organization: Organization Downsizing)
**Why not A:** Survivors often worry about future layoffs and feel less committed.
**Why not B:** Cutting staff without restructuring usually leads profits to decline.
**Why not D:** Downsizing can increase voluntary turnover, especially where firms invest little in staff.

questions.question: A firm must downsize and wants to limit the damage to the employees who stay. Which approach does the chapter recommend?

options.A: Avoid discussing it so that staff stay focused on their work
options.B: Cut training budgets first to show that everyone must sacrifice
options.C: Announce cuts suddenly to keep the rumours to a minimum
options.D: Communicate early, involve staff and offer assistance

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Effective downsizing strategies mirror organizational justice: invest in high-involvement practices afterward, communicate early, let employees participate (for example, through voluntary early retirement) and provide assistance such as severance and job search help. (Ch 13: The Leaner Organization: Organization Downsizing)
**Why not A:** Early communication helps employees feel their perspective is considered.
**Why not B:** Investing in high-involvement work practices afterward makes downsizing more effective.
**Why not C:** Discussing downsizing early reduces employees' worry.

questions.question: A consultant describes a firm with high specialization, rigid departments, narrow spans, centralization and high formalization. Which model is this, and what's its opposite?

options.A: Mechanistic; the organic model is flat and highly flexible
options.B: Virtual; the boundaryless model is its exact opposite
options.C: Organic; the mechanistic model is flat and flexible
options.D: Matrix; the simple structure is its exact opposite

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** The mechanistic model is essentially the bureaucracy; the organic model resembles the boundaryless organization: flat, with cross-functional and cross-hierarchical teams, free information flow, wide spans, decentralization and low formalization. (Ch 13: Why Do Structures Differ? Exhibit 13-5)
**Why not B:** The features listed define the mechanistic model, not a virtual one.
**Why not C:** This reverses the two models.
**Why not D:** The features listed define the mechanistic model.

questions.question: A tech firm's strategy is to introduce major new products ahead of its rivals. Which structure best fits this strategy?

options.A: Organic: loose, with low specialization and low formalization
options.B: A mix of tight controls now with loose new ventures later
options.C: Highly centralized with strict formalization of all work
options.D: Mechanistic: tight control and extensive specialization

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** An innovation strategy fits an organic structure (low specialization, low formalization, decentralized), though some mechanistic features can help rapid change happen smoothly. (Ch 13: Organizational Strategy, Exhibit 13-6)
**Why not B:** Mixing mechanistic and organic features fits an imitation strategy.
**Why not C:** Centralization and high formalization suit cost minimizers, not innovators.
**Why not D:** Tight, mechanistic control fits a cost-minimization strategy.

questions.question: A clothing retailer copies designer styles only after they've proven popular. Which strategy is this, and which structure fits it?

options.A: Cost minimization; mechanistic with high centralization
options.B: Imitation; mechanistic for current work, organic for new
options.C: Innovation; organic throughout, with low formalization
options.D: Imitation; organic for current work, mechanistic for new

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** An imitation strategy moves into new products or markets only after their viability is proven (like H&M); it combines tight mechanistic control of current activities with organic subunits for new undertakings. (Ch 13: Organizational Strategy, Exhibit 13-6)
**Why not A:** Cost minimizers sell basic products at low prices; this retailer follows proven trends.
**Why not C:** Copying proven styles is imitation, not innovation.
**Why not D:** This reverses the imitation structure.

questions.question: One firm grows from 300 to 800 employees; another grows from 2000 to 2500. Which growth will shift its structure more toward mechanistic, and why?

options.A: The smaller firm's, since size matters less past about 2000
options.B: Both equally, since each added exactly 500 employees
options.C: The larger firm's, since size matters more as firms expand
options.D: Neither, since size has little to do with structure

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Firms with 2000 or more employees tend to be more specialized and formalized, but size matters less as they expand: adding 500 to a 300-person firm shifts it much more than adding 500 to an already mechanistic 2000-person firm. (Ch 13: Organizational Size)
**Why not B:** The same increase matters far more to a smaller organization.
**Why not C:** Size becomes less important as an organization expands.
**Why not D:** Size significantly affects structure, especially in smaller firms.

questions.question: A custom furniture restorer and an automated car assembly plant use very different technologies. Which structures do they tend to prefer?

options.A: Both mechanistic, since all production needs tight control
options.B: Both organic, since technology doesn't affect structure
options.C: Restorer organic, plant mechanistic, given routineness
options.D: Restorer mechanistic, plant organic, given routineness

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Technologies differ in routineness: routine, standardized activities like assembly lines tend to favour mechanistic structures, while nonroutine, customized work like furniture restoring favours organic ones. (Ch 13: Technology)
**Why not A:** Nonroutine, customized work tends to favour organic structures.
**Why not B:** Organizational structures adapt to their technology.
**Why not D:** This reverses the technology–structure relationship.

questions.question: A firm faces scarce resources, rapid unpredictable change and many diverse competitors. How should it be structured?

options.A: More organically, since uncertainty is high
options.B: More mechanistically, to control the uncertainty tightly
options.C: It doesn't matter, since environment rarely affects design
options.D: As a simple structure run by one central decision maker

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** An environment's capacity, volatility and complexity determine uncertainty; the more scarce, dynamic and complex the environment, the more organic the structure should be, while abundant, stable and simple environments suit mechanistic structures. (Ch 13: Environment, Exhibit 13-7)
**Why not B:** High uncertainty calls for a more organic, flexible structure.
**Why not C:** The environment is a major determinant of structure.
**Why not D:** Centralizing all decisions in one person suits small firms, not highly uncertain environments.

questions.question: A highly educated professional seeking personal growth is placed in a narrow, repetitive role. What does the chapter predict?

options.A: Her productivity will keep rising indefinitely with practice
options.B: Negative reactions are most likely for people like her
options.C: Specialization never affects satisfaction, only output
options.D: She'll be more satisfied, since routine reduces her stress

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Specialization tends to raise productivity at the price of satisfaction; some people prefer routine, but negative outcomes are most likely in professional jobs held by people with high needs for growth and diversity. (Ch 13: Organizational Designs and Employee Behaviour)
**Why not A:** Productivity suffers once the diseconomies of repetitive work outweigh the gains.
**Why not C:** Specialization tends to reduce job satisfaction.
**Why not D:** Routine suits some people, but not those with high needs for growth.

questions.question: A director widens spans of control, expecting employees to perform better with more freedom. What does the evidence say?

options.A: Narrow spans reliably raise both performance and satisfaction
options.B: There's no clear link to employees' satisfaction or performance
options.C: Wider spans lower managers' own job satisfaction sharply
options.D: Wider spans reliably raise both performance and satisfaction

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** No evidence supports a relationship between span of control and employee satisfaction or performance; individual differences matter, and some evidence suggests managers' satisfaction rises as they supervise more people. (Ch 13: Organizational Designs and Employee Behaviour)
**Why not A:** No evidence links span of control either way to these outcomes.
**Why not C:** Some evidence suggests managers' satisfaction increases with more reports.
**Why not D:** Research fails to support the idea that wide spans improve performance.

questions.question: An HR team wants to know which structural feature is most strongly linked to employee job satisfaction. What does the evidence point to?

options.A: Wider spans of control, through more distant supervision
options.B: More departments, through greater work specialization
options.C: Higher formalization, through clearer and stricter rules
options.D: Less centralization, through greater autonomy

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** There's fairly strong evidence linking centralization and satisfaction: less centralized organizations give more autonomy, which is positively related to job satisfaction, though some people find autonomy frustratingly ambiguous. (Ch 13: Organizational Designs and Employee Behaviour)
**Why not A:** No evidence links span of control to employee satisfaction.
**Why not B:** Specialization tends to lower, not raise, satisfaction.
**Why not C:** The evidence ties satisfaction to decentralization and autonomy.

questions.question: Employees in a highly formalized, mechanistic firm and in a flexible, organic firm value different kinds of fairness. Which pairing fits the research?

options.A: Neither cares about fairness, only about autonomy levels
options.B: Mechanistic: fair procedures; organic: interpersonal justice
options.C: Mechanistic: interpersonal justice; organic: fair procedures
options.D: Both value only distributive fairness in pay outcomes

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** In highly formalized, mechanistic organizations, the fairness of formal policies and procedures strongly predicts satisfaction; in personal, adaptive organic organizations, employees value interpersonal justice more. (Ch 13: Organizational Designs and Employee Behaviour)
**Why not A:** Different kinds of fairness predict satisfaction in each structure.
**Why not C:** This reverses the findings.
**Why not D:** The research contrasts procedural and interpersonal fairness.

questions.question: A multinational opens offices in France and Greece. Based on the chapter, how are employees there likely to react to mechanistic structures?

options.A: They prefer boundaryless designs with no hierarchy at all
options.B: They tend to resist them more, given low power distance
options.C: They tend to accept them more, given their high power distance
options.D: Culture has no effect on how employees view structure

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** National culture influences preference for structure: employees from high power-distance cultures such as Greece, France and most of Latin America are much more accepting of mechanistic structures than those from low power-distance countries. (Ch 13: Global Implications, Culture and Employee Structure Preferences)
**Why not A:** High power-distance employees are more accepting of hierarchy.
**Why not B:** France and Greece are high, not low, in power distance.
**Why not D:** Research suggests national culture influences structure preferences.

questions.question: A manager lets a team work from home, but their tightly linked roles depend on each person predicting what the others will do next. What does research suggest?

options.A: The team's tasks matter more than how their roles connect
options.B: Remote work may cost them the benefits of teamwork
options.C: Working from home always improves performance in any job
options.D: Remote work removes any need for relationship building

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Work-from-home success depends on the job's structure more than its tasks; roles that need epistemic interdependence (predicting what others will do) require intentional relationship building, so teamwork benefits can be lost even when individuals do their tasks well. (Ch 13: Focus on Research, Working from Home)
**Why not A:** Success depends on the job's structure even more than on its tasks.
**Why not C:** Research suggests there are limits, depending on the person, job and culture.
**Why not D:** Intentional relationship building becomes even more important.

questions.question: Job candidates who prefer predictability tend to join mechanistic firms, while those who want autonomy end up in organic ones. What does this imply?

options.A: Firms should hire people who dislike their own structure
options.B: Everyone eventually prefers the organic structure most
options.C: Good matching reduces structure's effect on behaviour
options.D: Structure determines behaviour regardless of who is hired

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** People are attracted to, selected by and stay with organizations that suit their characteristics, so the effect of structure on behaviour is reduced when selection matches individual and organizational characteristics. (Ch 13: Organizational Designs and Employee Behaviour)
**Why not A:** Matching people to suitable structures is what reduces negative effects.
**Why not B:** Individuals differ; some prefer the predictability of mechanistic structures.
**Why not D:** Self-selection and matching reduce structure's effect on behaviour.
